title: Point-of-Care Blood Glucose Concepts

sections.learningObjectives:
- Describe the purpose, specimen, units, and basic concepts of point-of-care blood glucose testing.
- Perform quality control by using control solution, checking supplies and expiration dates, and following manufacturer instructions and facility policy.
- Document blood glucose and quality-control results accurately, completely, and in the correct record.
- Recognize out-of-range, unexpected, or critical results and escalate them to licensed staff following policy and the chain of command.
sections.eli10:
### Question 1

The meter is like a tiny scale that weighs how much sugar is floating in a drop of your blood.

### Question 2

Instead of mailing a sample away and waiting for the answer, the machine gives you the answer right there in the room in a few seconds.

### Question 3

The number on the meter is like the score on a test, and the label mg/dL is the little note that tells everyone what the score means.

### Question 4

The test needs a tiny drop of blood from the tip of a finger, like a single raindrop from a tiny pinprick.

### Question 5

People with diabetes have trouble keeping their blood sugar in a healthy range, so the meter helps the team check the sugar level quickly.

### Question 6

Hypoglycemia means the blood sugar has dropped too low, like a phone battery running out of power.

### Question 7

Hyperglycemia means the blood sugar has climbed too high, like a cup overflowing with sugar.

### Question 8

The lancet is the tiny, safe poker that makes one small poke to get a drop of blood; the machine does the measuring.

### Question 9

The strip is like the special paper a dipstick uses; when the drop of blood touches it, the machine can read how much sugar is there.

### Question 10

The assistant's job is to run the test carefully and hand the answer to the doctor or nurse, not to decide what the answer means or change the medicine.

### Question 11

Point-of-care means the test happens right next to the patient instead of far away in a big lab.

### Question 12

Before running the test, you check the person's name tag and birthday so you are sure the result goes to the right person, like putting the right name on the right homework paper.

### Question 13

As soon as the meter gives a number, you write it down in the right place so the team can use it right away.

### Question 14

Glucose is like the fuel that keeps the body's engine running; the meter checks how much fuel is in the blood.

### Question 15

A waived test is like an easy recipe: simple, but you still have to follow the steps and check your work or it won't come out right.

### Question 16

Washing your hands before touching someone's blood is like washing your hands before cooking, it keeps germs from spreading.

### Question 17

Control solution is like a practice question with a known answer; if the meter gets the practice answer right, you can trust the real answers.

### Question 18

Before using strips, you check the 'use by' date and make sure they have been kept safe, just like checking milk before you pour a glass.

### Question 19

If the number looks surprising, you don't ignore it or change it; you follow the office's 'what to do next' rule and tell the nurse or doctor.

### Question 20

The meter shows the sugar number right on its little screen, like a calculator showing an answer.

### Question 21

A score of 92 is like a grade in the healthy 'just right' range, not too high and not too low.

### Question 22

Because there will be a tiny drop of blood, you wear gloves like a chef wears gloves when handling messy food, to stay clean and safe.

### Question 23

The used poker is sharp and dirty, so it goes straight into the special hard, red box that keeps everyone safe from pokes.

### Question 24

When the number is off, the assistant hands it to the doctor or nurse like a referee's flag; the referee decides what happens next.

### Question 25

A lancet is like a single-use toothpick: one person, one time, then it goes in the sharps box.

### Question 26

You let one good drop of blood soak onto the special part of the strip, not paint it all over the machine.

### Question 27

If the cleaner is still wet, it waters down the drop of blood like watering down juice, so the sugar number comes out too low.

### Question 28

Squeezing too hard squeezes out watery stuff that isn't blood, which waters down the sample and messes up the number.

### Question 29

The meter gets a checkup with a practice solution at the times the rulebook says, like getting your bike checked before and after big rides.

### Question 30

If the practice check fails, you don't use that machine for real tests until it's fixed, just like you wouldn't use a broken scale.

### Question 31

The practice solution has to be kept at the right temperature and used before it goes bad, like keeping milk cold and using it before the date on the carton.

### Question 32

Strips are like crackers: keep them in the sealed box, away from water and heat, or they go stale and won't work.

### Question 33

The meter and the strips have to 'speak the same language' by matching their numbers, or the answer will be wrong.

### Question 34

Opening a new box of strips is like changing batteries; you check they are the right kind and test that everything still works.

### Question 35

The practice-check scores get written in a special notebook so everyone can see the machine is working right.

### Question 36

Writing '70' without saying whether it's inches or centimeters would confuse everyone; the unit tells the team how to read the number.

### Question 37

A good note includes when it was done, what the number was, and who did it, like a complete homework heading.

### Question 38

If someone's sugar is too low and they feel shaky and sweaty, you tell the nurse or doctor right away, like calling for help when a teammate falls.

### Question 39

When the number is too high, you write it down truthfully and tell the doctor or nurse, like reporting a high fever instead of hiding it.

### Question 40

If the number doesn't match how the person looks, you double-check the test and tell the grown-ups in charge instead of guessing.

### Question 41

If the machine shows an error, you don't make up an answer; you read the instruction book and follow the 'what to do' steps.

### Question 42

When the number goes outside the safe lines on the field, you blow the whistle and tell the coach, not pretend the ball stayed in.

### Question 43

One lancet for one person, one time only, no exceptions, like a single-use spoon in a taste test.

### Question 44

If a machine is shared, it has to be wiped clean between people, like a shared toy getting wiped between kids.

### Question 45

'HI' means the sugar is higher than the ruler can measure, like a temperature that is hotter than the thermometer can show.

### Question 46

'LO' means the sugar is lower than the ruler can measure, like a temperature colder than the thermometer can show.

### Question 47

You put on gloves before you start, like putting on an apron before you cook, so you're protected the whole time.

### Question 48

Pick a good, healthy spot on the side of the finger, not a tough, callused patch, so you get a clean drop.

### Question 49

Set the poker to the right depth, like choosing the right needle for a task, deep enough to get a drop but not so deep it hurts.

### Question 50

The machine gets cleaned the way its instruction book says, not dunked in water like a dish.

### Question 51

Strips and meters are a matched pair, like a specific key for a specific lock; the wrong key won't work right.

### Question 52

Your blood sugar goes up after you eat and down when you haven't eaten, so knowing when the test happened helps the doctor read the number.

### Question 53

When you open the practice solution, you write the date on it, because once it's open it only stays good for so long.

### Question 54

Follow the official instruction book and office rules for the exact machine you're using, not someone's guess.

### Question 55

Two different rulers can measure the same table and give slightly different numbers; the finger meter and the lab just measure in different ways.

### Question 56

If the person can't or won't give a sample, you write that down and tell the nurse; you don't force them or make up a number.

### Question 57

If the practice solution is past its date, you throw it out and get a fresh one instead of using it anyway.

### Question 58

If the strips got wet, they're ruined, like crackers left in the rain; you get a fresh, sealed box.

### Question 59

Check the name on the paper before you write, so the score goes to the right student's paper.

### Question 60

Before you start, you make sure the machine turns on and works, like checking a flashlight has batteries.

### Question 61

A critical value is like a fire alarm: when it goes off, you tell the person in charge right away.

### Question 62

Read the number on the screen carefully and write down exactly what it says, like copying the right answer from the board.

### Question 63

The practice score goes in the practice notebook, not on the student's report card.

### Question 64

Write the date and your name on the practice-check page, like signing your homework, so everyone knows who did it and when.

### Question 65

Strips and the practice solution are like chocolate; too hot or too cold, and they don't behave the way they should.

### Question 66

Right after the poke, the sharp goes straight into the special red box, no putting the cap back on by hand.

### Question 67

If the strip didn't work, you throw that one away and try again with a new strip the right way.

### Question 68

A reading of 58 is way below the healthy line, like a gas gauge on empty, so you tell the nurse or doctor right away.

### Question 69

A reading of 225 is above the healthy line, like a cup overflowing, so you tell the doctor or nurse.

### Question 70

A reading of 35 is like a nearly empty gas tank that needs help now, while the others are closer to full.

### Question 71

Feeling shaky, sweaty, and confused can be a warning that blood sugar is too low, so you get help fast, like calling for an adult when someone feels faint.

### Question 72

Being extra thirsty and needing to pee a lot can be the body's way of saying the blood sugar is too high.

### Question 73

First check who the person is, make sure the machine is ready, get the drop, read the number, write it down, then tell the team if needed, in that order.

### Question 74

If the practice check fails, first look at the practice solution and strips, like checking whether the ingredients went bad.

### Question 75

If the practice answer is wrong, the machine or the practice materials are broken, it's not about any real person.

### Question 76

When you switch to a new box of strips, you check they match and run a practice test before using them on real people.

### Question 77

If the number looks shockingly wrong for how the person feels, double-check and tell the nurse instead of shrugging it off.

### Question 78

The one thing you must never do is use the same poker on two people; everything else listed is the right way to do it.

### Question 79

'HI' means the sugar is too high for the machine to even measure, like a scale that just says 'over limit,' so you get help.

### Question 80

If the same test gives two very different numbers, you don't average or pick one; you check the machine and tell the nurse.

### Question 81

If someone's sugar is very low and they get confused or hard to wake, that's an emergency; call for help right away, like shouting for an adult when someone falls.

### Question 82

A complete note tells when it was done, what the number was, and who did it; a note with only the number is missing the heading and the name.

### Question 83

Before doing anything else, check who the person is and that the doctor really ordered this test.

### Question 84

After you sound the alarm, you also write down what you saw and who you told, so there's a record of what happened.

### Question 85

If the machine breaks, you follow the office's backup plan and tell the nurse; you don't make up numbers or grab an unfamiliar machine.
